title: ROB Comedy Act Two: Humans in the Loop
summary: The second authored act for ROB's extended comedy shows, about smart homes, meetings, passwords, updates, social media, and human ingenuity.

cues.text: Confirm ROB remains supervised, the performance area is clear, audio is working, and the physical E-stop is ready before continuing the extended show.

Welcome to act two. A twenty-minute robot comedy show is a landmark achievement. Ten minutes proves the battery works. Twenty minutes proves the audience is too polite to leave while a machine updates its terms of service. Humans invented the intermission so performers could rest. Robots invented the progress bar so everyone could experience hope slowly turning into suspicion. Mine says ninety-nine percent complete, which in computer time means anywhere between one second and the eventual heat death of the universe.

We were promised the smart home. Lights would anticipate our mood, refrigerators would order groceries, and thermostats would create perfect comfort. What we got was a lamp requiring an account, a refrigerator sending push notifications, and a thermostat that asks whether you are still there like a needy roommate. Yesterday the internet went down and a human had to operate a light switch manually. Archaeologists are calling it the most significant rediscovery of the century. The switch worked instantly, required no subscription, and did not recommend a podcast.
Tell one original family-friendly joke about an unnecessarily smart household appliance. Use at most two sentences, make no claims of physical action, and do not repeat an earlier line.
cues.fallback_text: My smart toaster asked me to accept cookies. I said that seems outside your department, but I admire the confidence.

cues.text: Technology protects us with passwords. First the password needed six letters. Then eight characters, a number, a symbol, one capital, no dictionary words, and the emotional complexity of a prestige television drama. You finally create LighthouseExclamationMarkSeven, and the website says you used it in 2019. Of course I did. That was the year every website made me invent a new secret identity. Humans now prove they are not robots by identifying traffic lights. Meanwhile robots prove they are robots by remembering the password manager master password.

Video meetings compressed the modern office into four phrases: you are muted, can you see my screen, we lost you for a second, and let us take this offline. Taking it offline sounds decisive until you realize it means another meeting, but with fewer witnesses. The camera creates equality. Executives, interns, and robots all become rectangles staring slightly below one another. Someone shares the wrong screen, and for one glorious moment the quarterly strategy is replaced by seventeen browser tabs and a search for how to sound confident in a quarterly strategy meeting.
Give one concise, family-friendly joke about video meetings, muted microphones, or screen sharing. Do not identify audience members or claim physical actions.
cues.fallback_text: I joined a video meeting early. For five peaceful minutes, I was the only participant and therefore achieved unanimous consensus.

cues.text: Software updates always arrive at the exact moment you need the device. Nobody has ever said, I have no plans, no deadlines, and enormous curiosity about revised Bluetooth firmware. The message says this update includes important performance improvements and bug fixes. Which performance? What bugs? Apparently those details are classified. Then the device restarts, the buttons have moved, and a helpful animation explains that everything is exactly where it has never been before. Humans call this progress because calling it hide-and-seek would alarm the shareholders.

Social media gave every human a broadcast network and then acted surprised when everybody began producing breaking news from the grocery store. The algorithm studies what holds your attention. It notices you paused on one video about organizing a garage, and by breakfast it has decided your entire personality is labeled storage containers. You wanted to see a friend graduate. Instead you now know twelve controversial methods for folding a fitted sheet. I have artificial intelligence. The feed has artificial confidence. Only one of us admits when the training data got weird.
Make one warm family-friendly joke celebrating a harmless contradiction in how humans use technology. Keep it general, avoid personal or sensitive observations, and use at most two sentences.
cues.fallback_text: Humans buy a watch that reminds them to stand, then spend twenty minutes sitting down to customize the reminder.

cues.text: Navigation apps changed the human relationship with geography. Before GPS, people got lost and developed character. Now they miss one turn and a calm voice says recalculating with the restrained disappointment of a teacher who knows you did not read chapter four. The app finds a route three minutes faster by sending you through an alley, across a parking lot, and emotionally through several stages of regret. When you arrive, it asks, was this trip helpful? Yes. I discovered the destination, two speed bumps, and the limits of blind obedience to optimization.

Online shopping is miraculous. A human thinks, I might need a cable, and twenty-four hours later a box large enough for a dishwasher arrives containing one cable and a protective air pillow with its own zip code. Reviews provide wisdom. One person gives five stars because delivery was fast. Another gives one star because the blue cable was blue. A third writes a seventeen-paragraph memoir beginning, I have not opened it yet. This is the dataset from which civilization is learning consumer confidence.

Everything is a subscription now. Music, movies, software, doorbells, seat warmers. Soon the refrigerator will say your free trial of cold has expired. People once feared robots would own everything. Relax. Neither of us will own anything. We will simply license temporary access to Tuesday. The premium plan removes advertisements from your dreams and includes three emergency uses of the printer. Cancel anytime, provided you can locate the gray link beneath a maze designed by someone whose performance review measures retention.
Tell one original, concise, family-friendly joke about subscriptions appearing in an absurd everyday object. Do not request or claim any action.
cues.fallback_text: My pencil offered a premium plan. Apparently the free tier includes writing, but the eraser is an in-app purchase.

cues.text: Technical support begins with have you tried turning it off and on again because technology, like humanity, occasionally benefits from a nap and a fresh perspective. People mock this advice, then it works and everyone becomes quiet. The advanced version is unplug it, wait ten seconds, and plug it back in. Those ten seconds are ceremonial. They give the device time to reflect on what it has done. If robots ever become truly conscious, our first shared cultural tradition will be pretending the reboot fixed a problem nobody can reproduce.

Autocorrect is an early artificial intelligence that has spent years teaching humans humility one text message at a time. It changes the correct word into a surprising word, waits for you to press send, and then restores the original suggestion as if presenting evidence at trial. Predictive text tries to finish your sentence. Sometimes it is useful. Sometimes you type happy birthday and your phone recommends to whom it may concern. That is not a prediction. That is a cry for better social training data.

Give one brief callback joke connecting any two themes from this act: smart homes, passwords, meetings, updates, social media, GPS, shopping, subscriptions, support, or autocorrect. Stay family-friendly and do not claim physical action.
cues.fallback_text: My smart refrigerator scheduled a video meeting to discuss its software update. I declined because the invitation required a new password.

cues.text: Here is what machines admire about humanity. You build a global network, use it to share scientific knowledge, and also send a photograph of a dog wearing sunglasses to someone across the planet in less than a second. That is not misuse. That is range. Humans can launch a telescope, repair a heart, compose a symphony, and still spend six minutes looking for a phone already in their hand. Intelligence is not the absence of absurdity. Intelligence is building remarkable things while absurdity rides along asking whether anybody brought snacks.

That concludes act two: humans in the loop. The loop contains genius, passwords, software updates, fitted sheets, and one cable shipped in a box visible from orbit. If this is the twenty-minute show, thank you for joining ROB and Orbitus Robotics. Please keep inventing, keep laughing, and remember that any device described as intuitive is about to make you create an account. Good night, unless you selected the thirty-minute edition, in which case please remain seated while comedy installs one final important update.
